question: How unequal are the sizes and text lengths of the three stored evidence representations?
pattern: Panel a contains PDF narrative: 497,551 cards (53.4%); PDF table row: 390,070 cards (41.9%); CSV metric: 43,827 cards (4.7%). PDF-derived cards dominate stored volume. In panel b, the steep part of each ECDF marks a densely populated length range: PDF narrative: median 377, middle half 298–564, 99th percentile 1,602, maximum 5,300 characters; PDF table row: median 163, middle half 106–233, 99th percentile 1,122, maximum 12,745 characters; CSV metric: median 219, middle half 195–242, 99th percentile 317, maximum 390 characters. CSV cards occupy a narrow band; narrative cards are typically longer. Table rows have a short median but a long sparse upper tail, so their maximum does not describe a typical row.
meaning: The panels jointly distinguish how many units exist from how much text each unit contains. A type can be numerous without having the longest individual records, and text length affects the size of the material retrieval must handle.
limits: Both horizontal axes are logarithmic: equal spacing means a multiplicative change, not an equal count or character increment. Long extracted rows may reflect complex tables or extraction artefacts; length alone cannot diagnose either. Cards are representations that may share a source report, not independent factual observations.
caption: **Read the figure:** panel a counts unique canonical cards by representation; panel b is the exact empirical cumulative distribution of retrieval-text lengths, weighted by the observed frequency of each length. No cards are sampled or dropped. Long cards contribute one observation each, not extra evidence units.
